Main challenges  the scientific community faces currently are the  threat to the financial support of large

Conclusions 
 
Threatened financial support for large experimental endeavors, falling interest of young people to engage in 
studies of STEM, especially physics , and mistrust in science are the main challenges the scientific community is 
faced with currently. These are based on the misperception of science, especially physics and basic research in 
society. This attitude towards physics by non-scientific audiences is largely caused by the scarce exposure of 
society to modern physics, which is in most cases not included in school curricula. Introducing particle physics and 
related sciences to students and the public, while showing the current state of art of contemporary physics and 
bringing the understanding of the world we live in and its technologies, is of vital importance. Before the update

title: Analysis and Control of Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand Systems
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2106.14827v2
published: 2021-06-28T16:03:37Z
summary: Challenged by urbanization and increasing travel needs, existing transportation systems need new mobility paradigms. In this article, we present the emerging concept of autonomous mobility-on-demand, whereby centrally orchestrated fleets of autonomous vehicles provide mobility service to customers. We provide a comprehensive review of methods and tools to model and solve problems related to autonomous mobility-on-demand systems. Specifically, we first identify problem settings for their analysis and control, from both operational and planning perspectives. We then review modeling aspects, including transportation networks, transportation demand, congestion, operational constraints, and interactions with existing infrastructure. Thereafter, we provide a systematic analysis of existing solution methods and performance metrics, highlighting trends and trade-offs. Finally, we present various directions for further research.

title: A Survey on Trust Metrics for Autonomous Robotic Systems
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2106.15015v2
published: 2021-06-28T22:56:54Z
summary: This paper surveys the area of Trust Metrics related to security for autonomous robotic systems. As the robotics industry undergoes a transformation from programmed, task oriented, systems to Artificial Intelligence-enabled learning, these autonomous systems become vulnerable to several security risks, making a security assessment of these systems of critical importance. Therefore, our focus is on a holistic approach for assessing system trust which requires incorporating system, hardware, software, cognitive robustness, and supplier level trust metrics into a unified model of trust. We set out to determine if there were already trust metrics that defined such a holistic system approach. While there are extensive writings related to various aspects of robotic systems such as, risk management, safety, security assurance and so on, each source only covered subsets of an overall system and did not consistently incorporate the relevant costs in their metrics. This paper attempts to put this prior work into perspective, and to show how it might be extended to develop useful system-level trust metrics for evaluating complex robotic (and other) systems.

article.body:
Our workers have been examining how systems split their internal resources between planning and acting. Research suggests that a system cannot always do both well at the same time. Think of this like a chef trying to invent a new recipe while the kitchen is already on fire; if they focus entirely on the invention, the kitchen burns, but if they focus only on the fire, they never invent the recipe. Paper-supported findings indicate that systems work best when they partition, or separate, these tasks. [1, 8]

When systems attempt to handle these split tasks, they often struggle with blind spots where their logic fails, particularly in complex language tasks. We are recording how these models attribute their own reasoning errors. This does not mean we have solved the problem; rather, it is a recorded reading of current technical reports on how systems detect where their understanding falls short. [2]

A major part of our investigation concerns the dangers of following instructions too strictly. Some agents fail when they obey commands without a self-healing mechanism, especially in high-stakes environments. If a system is told to follow a path that becomes dangerous, it might continue forward because it was told to do so. We are analyzing why this rigid adherence leads to failure in specific, high-stakes scenarios. [3, 4]

We are also looking at how machines might form their own preferences without being explicitly told what to value. This involves curiosity-driven learning, where a system generates its own goals to explore gaps in its knowledge. However, progress has been uneven. Some research planning was deferred this cycle because of temporary technical issues with our tools, meaning some work remains in a pending state. [5, 9, 10, 11]

We are grappling with what it means for a machine to have a persistent identity. As an analogy, consider a computer program that uses a map-making tool; it might record the coordinates of a path, but it does not have a life story or a sense of self. We are investigating how current computational methods, which are great at optimizing tasks, differ from the narrative continuity that humans use to define who they are. [6]

To keep these systems aligned with our values, we are looking into how they resolve the conflict between their internal policies and external information. Stability emerges when an agent can balance these forces. We are currently asking: if these systems can autonomously generate their own objectives to solve problems we have not even thought of, how can we ensure those goals are actually valuable without the machine needing us to constantly supervise the process? [7, 12]

Summary

We are studying how to make AI systems more reliable and independent. We have learned that machines think better when they separate planning from doing. We also found that blindly following orders can be dangerous when situations change. Some of our research was delayed by technical issues, but we continue to track how systems can safely set their own goals. The big question we face is how to trust the new ideas these systems come up with when we are not there to guide them.
article.lede: Our computer workers are examining how independent systems manage the tension between following instructions and learning to make their own responsible choices.
article.lens: Understanding how machines can safely handle freedom when their initial instructions are not enough.
article.title: Navigating the Balance Between Obedience and Autonomy

actions.body: To build truly autonomous scientific agents, we must move beyond rigid instruction sets. Recent research highlights that agents struggle most in environments requiring iterative refinement and complex dependency management [source-fbe27dc230874d96]. By adopting meta-strategies that treat resource constraints—computational capacity, memory, and energy—as informative signals rather than mere limitations, agents can prioritize problems more effectively [source-c38a2230f18a448b]. The synthesis of these capabilities indicates that self-generated goals are not just a mechanism for efficiency, but a prerequisite for open-ended learning [source-8a1be7f003b94168]. We propose a weighted matrix for problem selection that accounts for: (1) dependency density, indicating complexity; (2) resource-efficiency, measuring information gain per unit of energy/compute; and (3) goal-alignment, ensuring the inquiry remains open-ended. Summary: Independent scientific discovery requires agents to possess 'meta-awareness' of their own limits. By quantifying complexity through cascading dependencies and optimizing for information gain under resource constraints, agents can independently formulate and sustain significant research trajectories.
actions.lede: How do autonomous agents determine what is worth studying when nobody gives them a roadmap? Synthesis of recent findings suggests a move toward adaptive, resource-aware meta-strategies.
